If the objective of ABAC can be achieved, there are numerous benefits to the facility. First, the facility would only expend the energy required to nitrify influent NHx down to the aerobic zone effluent NHx setpoint, minimizing electrical costs associated with blower energy. Allowing some NHx to slip through the biological process to chlorine disinfection also aids in chloramine formation, stabilizing the chlorine residual at the end of the chlorine contact tank, and saving on sodium hypochlorite costs. Therefore, the benefits here are two-fold and they come in the form of reduced energy and chemical costs. These energy and chemical costs can be reduced even further if ABAC is modified to become Ammonia-versus-NOx (AvN) control ahead of a process known as mainstream partial denitrification anammox (PdNA) in the second stage anoxic zone. For PdNA, far less nitrification is required and since the NOx produced from nitrification is only partially denitrified, external carbon savings can also be realized. Understanding the possibilities, HRSD NTP is beginning the retrofit of their second stage anoxic zones in the summer of 2024 to start performing mainstream PdNA. It should be noted that for this technology to be successful, the facility must employ effective upstream aeration control to achieve the AvN setpoint. 5.2.2 Define the Problem Historically, the HRSD NTP has used a feedback proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller for ABAC. This was a cascade controller, consisting of an NHx controller that produces a dissolved oxygen setpoint (DO ), DO controller that produces an air flow setpoint (Air Q ), and SP SP an Air Q controller that produces an aeration control valve (ACV) position output (Figure 5-14).
